title: MASAI randomized trial in southwest Sweden: Transpara-supported mammography screening finds more cancers with less screen reading, at a non-inferior interval cancer rate
summary: In the MASAI trial of 105,934 women, Transpara-supported screening found 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading. It cut screen reading by 44.2%.
headline: *Transpara* helps Swedish breast screening find more cancers
metric: a detection rate of 6.4 per 1,000 against 5.0 per 1,000
brief: Lund University researchers ran the MASAI trial within the Swedish national screening program. Between 12 April 2021 and 7 December 2022, they randomly assigned 105,934 women in southwest Sweden to Transpara-supported screening or to a control group. In the control group, two radiologists without AI did standard double reading. The AI group had 6.4 screen-detected cancers per 1,000 women against 5.0 in the control group. It needed 44.2% fewer screen readings.[1] Results for the primary outcome, the rate of interval cancers, appeared in The Lancet in 2026. The rate was 1.55 per 1,000 with AI and 1.76 per 1,000 without. That result met the trial's non-inferiority margin. The difference was not statistically significant.[2] The trial tested one product in one region. Its design does not separate the effect of the triage by risk score from that of the marks on suspicious areas.[3]

title: ScreenTrustCAD at Capio Sankt Göran Hospital, Stockholm: Lunit Insight MMG as a third reader leads to 19 more screen-detected breast cancers than two radiologists
summary: In Stockholm, Lunit's Insight MMG read 55,581 mammograms beside two radiologists, and the three together found 269 cancers against 250 by the radiologists alone.
headline: *Insight MMG* as a third reader finds more breast cancers in Stockholm
metric: the three together found 269 cancers against 250 by the radiologists alone
brief: The ScreenTrustCAD study measured what an AI reader adds where breast screening already uses two radiologists.[1] Karolinska Institutet researchers ran it at Capio Sankt Göran Hospital in Stockholm. From 1 April 2021 to 9 June 2022, Lunit's Insight MMG ran in the background on the screening mammograms of 55,581 women. Two radiologists alone would have found 250 cancers. With the AI as a third reader, 269 were found. In the paired design, two radiologists and the AI read the examinations independently. The 19 extra cancers therefore came from examinations that only the AI flagged.[2] The researchers also found that one radiologist with AI was non-inferior to two radiologists, with 261 cancers against 250. The study ran at one hospital with one mammography vendor. Lunit was among its funders.[3]

title: Nigeria's Rapid Response Register used machine-learning maps of poverty to select 1,163 urban wards for cash transfers in response to COVID-19
summary: Nigeria used machine-learning poverty maps from satellite imagery to select 1,163 of its poorest urban wards for a COVID-19 cash transfer that counted 49,000 beneficiary households by 15 October 2021.
headline: Nigeria uses machine-learning poverty maps to direct COVID-19 cash aid
metric: 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021
brief: Nigeria had no urban social registry. Its National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office therefore built the Rapid Response Register for a government-funded cash transfer during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government used maps of poverty by ward, made by applying machine-learning algorithms to satellite imagery. With them it selected 1,163 of the poorest urban wards, with a population of over 20 million.[1] Their residents then registered by mobile phone and were verified in person. The developers of the maps report that, in targeting the poor, their machine-learning approach raises precision at the ward level to 0.92. A survey-based benchmark reaches 0.79.[2] No source shows how many people the maps helped. A World Bank status report of 29 January 2025 records 49,000 beneficiary households in the cash transfer as of 15 October 2021. The World Bank does not say how many of them had been paid. It also counts over 5 million households supported by the program of direct benefit transfers. It gives no breakdown of the share that the register targeted.[3] Human Rights Watch researchers argued in July 2021 that the targeting methods had in all likelihood excluded, or would exclude, large numbers of people in need.[4]

title: Baricitinib, identified with BenevolentAI's knowledge graph, lowered COVID-19 deaths in the RECOVERY trial
summary: BenevolentAI researchers used the Benevolent Platform's knowledge graph to identify baricitinib for COVID-19, and in the RECOVERY trial mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone.
headline: Drug found with a knowledge graph lowered COVID-19 deaths in a trial
metric: mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone
brief: On 4 February 2020 BenevolentAI researchers reported in The Lancet that their knowledge graph had helped them identify a possible treatment for COVID-19. It was baricitinib, an arthritis drug. In the ACTT-2 trial, 1,033 hospitalized adults received remdesivir with either baricitinib or a placebo. Median recovery took 7 days with baricitinib and 8 days with the placebo. In the COV-BARRIER trial, 8% of patients receiving baricitinib had died by day 28, compared with 13% receiving a placebo. Mortality was a secondary outcome in that trial. The trial did not meet its primary outcome of reduced disease progression.[1] In the later RECOVERY trial, 8,156 patients were randomly assigned to usual care with or without baricitinib. Mortality, its primary outcome, was 12% with baricitinib and 14% with usual care alone.[2] On 14 January 2022 the World Health Organization strongly recommended baricitinib with corticosteroids. The recommendation covered patients severely or critically ill with COVID-19. On 10 May 2022 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved baricitinib for hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who need supplemental oxygen or other respiratory support. The European Medicines Agency reached the provisional opinion that three trials did not conclusively show meaningful benefit. Eli Lilly then withdrew its European application on 7 December 2022.[3] None of the trials compared discovery with AI against discovery without it. The knowledge graph's part in the choice rests on a letter and a methods paper by BenevolentAI researchers.[4]

title: Detection by a Fitbit Sense ECG leads to diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia
summary: A Fitbit Sense watch detected an irregular heart rate of 164 beats per minute in a man in Jamshedpur, India. He was treated for ventricular tachycardia after he sought care.
headline: Doctors treat ventricular tachycardia after Fitbit flags a fast heart
metric: detected an irregular heart rate of 164 beats per minute with irregular rhythm
brief: In October 2021 a 55-year-old man in Jamshedpur, India, had symptoms at work. His Fitbit Sense showed an irregular rhythm at 164 beats per minute. He felt the need to visit a doctor immediately and went to Tata Main Hospital. Cardiologists there diagnosed idiopathic fascicular ventricular tachycardia from a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and further tests. They restored sinus rhythm by electrical cardioversion. On verapamil, he was later reported to be doing well.[1] The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the watch's ECG app to tell atrial fibrillation from sinus rhythm. Ventricular tachycardia lies outside the rhythms that it was cleared to classify.[2] The benefit also rests on an assumption that he would have waited longer without the reading. A single case report leaves no way to check it.

headline: ASENA flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives
metric: 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive
brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged the car. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets of factory-made explosive, 52.5 kg in all. The explosive was assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. It sentenced four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for the same offense.[2] ASENA was designed to flag drug crime. This find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs. He said that the police had used analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”.[3] The head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department spoke in June 2022. He listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source records the data that ASENA matched for this car. None of the sources says whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no informant is reported.[5]

brief: The Department of Justice reported on 30 June 2025 that its analysts and their collaborators had detected anomalous Medicare billing in Operation Gold Rush. According to the American Hospital Association, accountable care organizations had also reported the suspect billing for intermittent urinary catheters.
